offres.titre: Advisor, Partnerships - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029
offres.description:
Advisor, Partnerships - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029 
The Advisor, Partnerships contributes to the development and effective management of the strategic partnerships, serving as the SIED coordination point with priority external partners, new funding opportunities and partnership-related initiatives. The position plays a key role in enhancing engagement with a range of partners, with the overall aim of maximizing impact and value for money.
A key focus of the role is the coordination of specific externally financed initiatives and set-asides, maintaining a consolidated view of different arrangements and ensuring consistency in how these are designed, established and managed across partners. The role acts as a coordination point across Global Fund Secretariat relevant business owners and enabling functions, helping connect funding with strategic priorities and implementation realities, and ensuring appropriate processes, accountabilities and ways of working are established while recognizing the requirements of individual partners. 
The role also serves as a strategic focal point for the External Relations and Communications Division (ERCD) on new funding opportunities, helping connect potential partner funding with organizational priorities and coordinating engagement across relevant teams. The role supports the assessment and development of new opportunities, ensuring strategic, programmatic and operational perspectives are brought together early and that there is a clear pathway from initial opportunity through decision-making, design and country-level implementation. 
The role also provides direct support to the Manager and SIED leadership on priority external engagements. This includes developing engagement strategies and objectives; coordinating and consolidating inputs from across the Secretariat; preparing briefings, presentations and other materials for senior-level engagements; and capturing feedback, commitments and follow-up actions to ensure engagements translate into coordinated organizational action. 
Through these responsibilities, the role maintains an integrated view of the Global Fund’s strategic partnership landscape, identifies connections and emerging opportunities across engagements, and supports the Manager and SIED leadership to manage increasingly complex external relationships in a coherent, strategic and disciplined way. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 Strategic Partnership Coordination: 
 Coordinate SIED’s strategic partnership portfolio, maintaining an integrated view of priority external relationships, initiatives, commitments and opportunities; identifying connections, dependencies and emerging issues; and supporting coherent engagement across SIED and the wider Secretariat.
 Build and maintain effective relationships with priority external partners, working across foundations, bilateral and multilateral organizations, technical agencies and other partners to advance shared priorities and maximize the impact and value of partnership opportunities.
 Externally Financed Initiatives & Set-Asides:  
 Coordinate specific externally financed initiatives and set-asides, working across business owners and enabling functions to support their design, establishment and implementation and maintain consolidated oversight of objectives and timelines.  
 Engage in dialogue and negotiations with bilateral and multilateral partners to identify and leverage additional resources at the central, regional and country levels to support program planning and implementation
 Drive greater consistency in the management of set-asides and externally financed initiatives, developing common processes and ways of working where appropriate, while accommodating the specific requirements of individual partners; identify and apply lessons across arrangements to continuously improve the Global Fund’s approach.  
 Coordinate emerging and existing platforms from bilateral and technical partners such as the Impact Through Partnerships Partner Support Platform and Joint Working Group to address issues of program design and implementation. 
 New Funding Opportunities: 
 Serve as SIED’s strategic focal point for ERCD on new funding opportunities, coordinating the assessment and development of opportunities and bringing together strategic, programmatic, country and operational perspectives to assess alignment with Global Fund priorities, potential impact and implementation feasibility.  
 Coordinate the pathway from funding opportunity to implementation, working with ERCD, GMD and relevant SIED and enabling functions to ensure clear ownership, decision-making and hand-offs from initial partner discussions through design and approval to country-level implementation.  
 Implementation Tracking & Partner Dialogue:  
 Track implementation of priority partnership initiatives and commitments, working with Grant Management, SIED and other relevant teams to maintain visibility of progress, results, emerging risks and delivery bottlenecks.  
 Identify programmatic and cross-cutting bottlenecks where partner engagement can help unlock delivery, working closely with the Data, Analytics and Learning Department, implementation experience and country insights to determine where additional technical, financial or other partner support could have greatest value.  
 Use these insights to drive focused dialogue and problem-solving with partners, connecting identified needs with available partner capabilities and resources, coordinating follow-up across relevant teams, and tracking whether agreed actions are addressing bottlenecks and supporting improved implementation and scale-up. 
 Strategic Engagement & Management Support: 
 Support the Manager and SIED leadership to develop and execute engagement strategies for priority external partners, defining objectives and desired outcomes, identifying key messages and issues, and ensuring engagements are aligned with broader organizational priorities and relationships.  
 Coordinate preparation and follow-through for senior external engagements, consolidating inputs and feedback from across the Secretariat; preparing briefings, presentations and other materials; and tracking commitments, decisions and follow-up actions to ensure engagements translate into coordinated organizational action. 
 Subject to change by the Executive Director at any time at their sole discretion. 
 Qualifications

 Advanced university degree in public health, administration or management.
 Experience 
 Essential: 
 Experience in developing and coordinating strategic partnerships, including working in foundations, bilateral and multilateral organizations, technical agencies and/or other external partners.
 Demonstrated experience coordinating complex, cross-functional initiatives, bringing together strategic, programmatic, financial and operational perspectives
 Demonstrated experience tracking implementation and identifying delivery bottlenecks, using data and implementation insights to support problem-solving and focused dialogue with partners.
 Experience supporting senior-level external engagement, including developing engagement strategies, preparing high-quality briefings and materials, coordinating organizational positions and ensuring effective follow-through.

offres.titre: Specialist, New Product Introduction & Integration, ICSC, Supply Operations - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029
offres.description:
Specialist, New Product Introduction & Integration, ICSC, Supply Operations - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029 
The Global Fund aims to accelerate the end of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria as epidemics, while increasing access to quality-assured health products and services at affordable and sustainable prices. Within the Secretariat, Supply Operations plays a central role in sourcing, procurement, quality assurance and supply chain matters, including strategy formulation and implementation, policy development, innovation, sustainability, new product introduction and country capacity building. The In-Country Supply Chain (ICSC) team leads the Global Fund's work to strengthen national health supply chains, particularly in countries with under-developed supply chain infrastructure and management systems, so that health products procured through Global Fund grants reach people reliably, efficiently and sustainably.
The Specialist, New Product Introduction & Integration, ICSC leads the Global Fund’s work to strengthen country supply chain readiness for the introduction, scale-up and sustainable integration of new health products, technologies and innovations across national health systems. Under the supervision of the Manager, In-Country Supply Chain Strategy, Policy & Initiatives, the Specialist works across planning, digital, governance, monitoring and service delivery domains to ensure that countries can effectively plan for, adopt, deploy and institutionalize innovations from introduction through scale-up and routine implementation in an integrated manner.
The role supports Country Teams and national stakeholders to translate innovation opportunities into scalable, sustainable and country-owned solutions by addressing the policy, regulatory, market, financing, digital, operational, workforce and governance requirements for successful adoption. It contributes to relevant strategic initiatives and catalytic investments and works closely with internal teams, technical partners and country stakeholders to move innovations from global recommendation and early introduction to routine use.
The position requires strong expertise in new product introduction, implementation planning and health supply chains, combined with the ability to lead complex, cross-functional initiatives in diverse country contexts. The remit is product agnostic and may cover medicines, diagnostics, prevention products, devices, digital tools and other health technologies or delivery innovations. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 The main responsibilities of the Specialist, New Product Introduction & Integration, ICSC include:
 1. Lead the new product introduction ICSC strategy and portfolio approach 
 Provide coherent technical leadership for product-agnostic introduction and scale-up, by:
 •     Supporting countries and Country Teams to develop costed, risk-informed and sequenced NPI roadmaps, including accountabilities, milestones, readiness actions and scale-up pathways.
 •     Developing and maintaining an ICSC approach, readiness framework, tools and guidance for the introduction, scale-up and institutionalization of new health products, technologies and innovations.
 •     Monitoring relevant innovation pipelines and translating emerging opportunities into clear implications for country supply chains, health systems and Global Fund investments.
 •     Promoting a portfolio approach that captures cross-product lessons, avoids fragmented introduction efforts and strengthens reusable country and NPI capabilities.
 2. Support ICSC country readiness assessments and introduction planning 
 Enable countries to move from policy intent to implementation, by:
 •     Leading or supporting country readiness assessments covering policy and regulatory requirements, demand, supply chain, financing, digital systems, service delivery, workforce, governance and stakeholder coordination.
 •     Advising on public, private and mixed-channel delivery approaches, taking account of quality, access, affordability, regulation, reporting and equity.
 •     Ensuring introduction plans are country-owned, aligned with national strategies and designed for progressive transition into routine systems.
 •     Advising on sustainable transition arrangements, including the financing of enabling systems, technical support and ongoing operational costs.
 3. Drive supply chain preparedness and operational integration 
 Ensure that national supply chains can reliably support introduction and scale-up, by:
 •     Generating market intelligence on channel capacity, provider readiness, access barriers and risks that may affect product uptake or availability.
 •     Supporting development of fit-for-purpose supply and distribution strategies, including channel selection, launch phasing, safety stock, replenishment and transition from legacy products where relevant.
 •     Identifying operational bottlenecks, dependencies and risks and ensuring that practical mitigation measures are built into introduction and scale-up plans.
 •     Supporting integration of new products into routine planning, operating procedures, logistics systems, performance management and institutional accountabilities.
 4. Design digital, data and performance management 
 Ensure that decisions and implementation are supported by appropriate information, by:
 •     Defining data requirements and performance indicators for readiness, availability, uptake, coverage, equity, cost and implementation progress.
 •     Supporting integration of new products into national logistics, program and health information systems, avoiding parallel systems wherever feasible.
 •     Advising on interoperability, product master data, traceability, dashboards and analytics requirements in coordination with relevant digital and data teams.
 •     Using implementation evidence to identify corrective actions, inform scale-up decisions and strengthen accountability for results.
 5. Deliver and manage related Catalytic Investments 
 Contribute to the effective design, delivery and measurement of catalytic funding, by:
 •     Managing assigned workplans and deliverables under Catalytic Investments, including technical partner selection, contracting inputs, oversight of deliverables, and monitoring of progress and results.
 •     Preparing briefing materials, syntheses and internal recommendations for Secretariat leadership, governance bodies and donors.
 •     Enabling cross-portfolio learning, identifying best practices and supporting their scale-up across countries.
 6. Provide advisory support and coordinate with stakeholders 
 Act as a recognized source of expertise within and beyond the Secretariat, by:
 •     Providing structured guidance and analysis to Country Teams on supply chain financing, costing and optimization questions arising in country dialogue, funding requests, grant making and implementation.
 •     Serving as an effective interface with other Supply Operations teams, the Grant Management Division, Health Finance, Technical Advice and Partnerships, Risk and other relevant functions.
 •     Engaging with external partners, including the Gates Foundation, the World Bank (including Global Financing Facility), Gavi, UNICEF, UNITAID, WHO, bilateral partners and technical assistance providers, on supply chain financing and costing matters.
 •     Contributing to internal and external training and guidance on Global Fund in-country supply chain policies, tools and approaches.
 Subject to change by the Executive Director at any time at their sole discretion. 
 Qualifications 
 Essential :
 •     Advanced university degree in information systems, computer science, engineering, supply chain management, public health or another relevant field.
 Desirable :
 •     Qualification in digital health, data science or supply chain management.
 Experience 
 Essential: 
 Substantial relevant professional experience, typically eight to ten years, in global health, health

offres.titre: Specialist, ICSC Digital Public Goods, Supply Operations - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029
offres.description:
Specialist, ICSC Digital Public Goods, Supply Operations - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029 
The Global Fund aims to accelerate the end of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria as epidemics, while increasing access to quality-assured health products and services at affordable and sustainable prices. Within the Secretariat, Supply Operations plays a central role in sourcing, procurement, quality assurance and supply chain matters, including strategy formulation and implementation, policy development, innovation, sustainability, new product introduction and country capacity building. The In-Country Supply Chain (ICSC) team leads the Global Fund's work to strengthen national health supply chains, particularly in countries with under-developed supply chain infrastructure and management systems, so that health products procured through Global Fund grants reach people reliably, efficiently and sustainably.
The Specialist, ICSC Digital Public Goods accelerates supply chain digitalization through shared digital public goods (DPGs). Under the supervision of the Manager, In-Country Supply Chain Strategy, Policy and Initiatives, the Specialist leads the ICSC team's work on campaign management tools for insecticide-treated net (ITN) and other health campaigns (including DIGIT HCM), supply chain costing models and tools, traceability, and quantification and analytics tools.
This role complements the ICSC team's existing digitalization role, which supports the implementation of core systems financed in grants (eLMIS, ERP and WMS installation and scale-up). The Specialist, Digital Public Goods focuses instead on the shared, reusable digital assets that sit above and alongside core systems: open, standards-based tools that multiple countries can adopt, adapt and sustain, reducing duplication and cost across the portfolio.
The position requires strong expertise in digital health and supply chain information systems, digital public goods and open-source ecosystems, data standards and interoperability, and the management of technology deployments in low-resource settings. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 The main responsibilities of the Specialist, ICSC Digital Public Goods include:
 1. Lead the strategy and stewardship of shared digital public goods 
 Ensure a coherent portfolio approach to shared digital assets for supply chains, by:
 Developing and maintaining the ICSC strategy for shared digital public goods, including selection criteria, governance, total cost of ownership and sustainability considerations.
 Coordinating with global DPG ecosystems, product owners and funders to shape roadmaps that reflect country and Global Fund needs.
 Advising on data governance, hosting, licensing and country ownership arrangements for shared tools.
 Ensuring complementarity with the core systems workstream (eLMIS, ERP, WMS) so that shared tools integrate with, rather than duplicate, national systems.
 These shared digital public goods can cover some of the key areas outlined below, but are not limited to only these thematic areas.
 1A. Campaign digitalization 
 Improve the efficiency, accountability and coverage of mass campaigns, by:
 Providing Global Fund support for ITN campaign digitalization, including deployment of campaign management platforms such as DIGIT HCM for micro-planning, household registration, distribution tracking, stock management and real-time monitoring.
 Supporting countries and Country Teams in platform selection, implementation planning, geospatial and supply chain integration, and capacity building for national teams.
 Working with partners (including the Alliance for Malaria Prevention, Malaria Consortium, eGov Foundation and other implementers) to align approaches, share learning and expand cross-campaign use of digital tools.
 Tracking and reporting the results of campaign digitalization, including commodity accountability, wastage reduction and coverage equity.
 1B. Supply chain costing models and analytics tools 
 Equip countries and the Secretariat with shared analytical tools, by:
 Leading the development, maintenance and country deployment of supply chain costing models and tools, in close coordination with the ICSC financing and optimization workstream.
 Building analytics capability on top of grant-funded systems, including dashboards and cross-country benchmarking datasets.
 1C. Traceability of health products 
 Strengthen end-to-end visibility and product security, by:
 Supporting countries in developing pragmatic traceability roadmaps for health products, including adoption of GS1 and related data standards, verification approaches and phased track-and-trace implementation.
 Coordinating traceability work with sourcing, procurement, quality assurance, regulatory partners and manufacturers to ensure coherence from global supply through to in-country distribution.
 Overseeing the sourcing strategy, selection and adoption of a fit-for-purpose traceability solution for the Global Fund and countries as needed and supporting country implementation, as needed, with due consideration for interoperability, scalability, sustainability and value for money.
 Documenting cost, feasibility and impact evidence to guide Global Fund policy and country investment decisions on traceability.
 1D. Quantification and Analytics tools for forecasting and supply planning: 
 Design, governance and rollout of approaches and control-tower capabilities connecting demand, supply, inventory and shipment data.
 Engagement in the Funders Forum's "Future of Planning" workstream — representing Global Fund and country needs in the convergence of next-generation planning tools, and ensuring resulting tools are stewarded as shared DPGs.
 Interoperability of planning tools with national systems and procurement/order management platforms.
 Sustainable stewardship arrangements for planning tools (hosting, maintenance, helpdesk, financing) as the funder landscape evolves.
 Country adoption of quantification and analytics tools for forecasting and supply planning, aligned with partner tools and national quantification processes.
 2. Support interoperability and country data ecosystems 
 Ensure shared tools strengthen, rather than fragment, national data systems, by:
 Promoting standards-based interoperability between shared digital public goods and national systems (eLMIS, DHIS2, ERP, WMS), including through open standards and API-based integration.
 Advising Country Teams on digital health investments in funding requests and grants to maximize reuse of shared assets and avoid duplication.
 Contributing to internal and external training and guidance on supply chain digitalization, digital public goods and data use.
 3. Deliver Catalytic Investments and coordinate with stakeholders 
 Ensure effective delivery of Catalytic Investment funding and coherent partner engagement, by:
 Managing assigned workplans and deliverables under catalytic investments, including technical partner selection and oversight, monitoring of progress and synthesis of results for leadership and governance audiences.
 Serving as an effective interface with other Supply Operations teams, the Grant Management Division, Technical Advice and Partnerships, the Data and Digital Health functions and other relevant teams.
 Engaging with external partners, including the Gates Foundation, WHO, the Digital Public Goods Alliance ecosystem, technology providers and technical assistance partners.
 Subject to change by the Executive Director at any time at their sole discretion. 
 Qualifications 
 Essential: 
 Advanced university degree in information systems, computer science, engineering, supply chain management, public health or another relevant field.
 Desirable: 
 Qualification in digital health, data science or supply chain management.
 Experience 
 Essential: 
 Substantial relevant professional experience (typically eight to ten years) in digital health, supply chain information systems and/or health supply chain manag

offres.titre: Specialist, Non-Global Fund Financed Procurement Performance Management & Reporting - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2028
offres.description:
Specialist, Non-Global Fund Financed Procurement Performance Management & Reporting - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2028 
The Global Fund aims to accelerate the end of AIDS, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria as epidemics. As part of our mandate to fight the three diseases, the Global Fund plays a leading role in global markets for medicines and technologies that prevent, diagnose, and treat HIV, Tuberculosis and Malaria. Every year, more than half of the Global Fund’s investments is used to procure key health products, ensuring they are available to those who need them most. 
As one of the biggest health product procurement entities in the public sector, investing nearly US$2 billion annually in health products and equipment procurement, the Global Fund is uniquely placed to drive equitable access to quality-assured health products, services and innovations through its Supply Operations department. 
Supply Operations, collaborating across the Global Fund Secretariat, is responsible for the Global Fund’s market shaping activities and the overall management of health product sourcing, procurement, quality assurance and supply chains. 
The Value Delivery function is a central team in the Supply Operations Front Office to support Supply Operations leadership & emerging strategy, drive transformation and change initiatives, facilitate annual planning, budget and workforce management, foster operational excellence, and connect end-to-end data analytics, insights and compliance monitoring. 
Non-Global Fund Financed Procurement (NGFP) enables eligible buyers and financing partners to access quality-assured health and non-health products through the Pooled Procurement Mechanism (PPM) and wambo.org using funding other than Global Fund grants, with an expected medium term transaction volume of up to USD ~1 billion.

Program Delivery Specialist, Sustainability and Transition, GMD - GL D - Temporary until December 2027 - French Speaking 
The Global Fund aims to accelerate the end of AIDS, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria as diseases of public health importance. The organization invests more than US$4 billion a year to support programs run by local experts in countries and communities most in need. Since 2020, through the COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM), additional funding has been made available to support countries to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 and build resilient community and public health systems. 
The Global Fund’s Grant Management Division (GMD), in collaboration with teams across the Global Fund Secretariat, is responsible for the overall management of the Global Fund’s grant investments at country and regional level, driving impact in implementing countries. It provides leadership and strategic direction to the Global Fund’s country operations and drives the translation of the GF strategy into operational milestones at global, regional, and country portfolio level, including signing grants, making disbursements, regular portfolio monitoring and oversight. It works in a complex and rapidly evolving environment with implementing partners, including Principal Recipients (PRs), sub-recipients (SRs), Country Coordinating Mechanisms (CCM), in-country health sector and humanitarian clusters, multiple stakeholders from public, private sectors and communities to drive success on the ground and manage the growth in portfolio investments value, expanding breadth and depth of program and systems strengthening interventions, sophistication of program design, data driven decision making, differentiated approaches, intensified program quality focus, and introduction of new health products, services and interventions.
Maximizing people-centered integrated systems for health is a core objective of the Global Fund Strategy, which aims to end HIV, TB, and Malaria (HTM) and address broader health needs. The Global Fund has become the world’s largest multilateral provider of grants to build resilient and sustainable systems for health (RSSH) and pandemic preparedness and response (PPR) capabilities, investing US$1.5 billion a year in public and community health systems between 2021 and 2023 through HTM grants and the COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM). 
The Global Fund continues to support the efficient and effective implementation of public health approaches through strategic engagement in Africa and the Middle East. The focus is on country public and community health capacity strengthening & building efficient, agile, people-centered, and sustainable national health systems which are critical for the fight against HTM. Grant investments aim to ensure equitable access to integrated services, quality assured and affordable health products, and improved overall health service delivery to vulnerable populations, including pregnant women and children and key and vulnerable populations. Multiple countries across Africa and the Middle East are scaling up these approaches through strategically prioritized portfolio investments, while simultaneously facing significant sustainability and transition challenges as external financing landscapes evolve.

They will guide capacity-building efforts, and coordination of relevant technical assistance to strengthen countries’ ability to effectively and efficiently implement their sustainability and transition agendas. The Program Delivery Specialist will also lead the development and socialization of an AME learning agenda for implementation of sustainability and transition objectives both internally as well as between countries (in collaboration with other stakeholders), including promoting the exchange of lessons learned, good practices, and innovative approaches to strengthen programmatic outcomes, implementation effectiveness, the long-term sustainability and resilience of national health programs, and successful transition planning and outcomes.
The Program Delivery Specialist will be based in a regional team in the Grant Management Division (GMD) and will collaborate with members of Country Teams (e.g. S/FPM, S/PO, PHME, HPM), other Implementation Specialists in the region, and relevant functional specialists in the Health Finance Department, Technical Advice and Partnership Department (TAP), CRG Department, and other teams as relevant to advance grant implementation and achievement of results for the assigned country portfolios.

 Facilitate dialogue to align sustainability and transition priorities, integrate innovations with countries’ operational plans and enhance in-country mechanisms for governance, monitoring, execution and technical support.
 Identify opportunities for integration and data sharing to promote efficiency and improve quality of planning and implementation.
 2. Support for high quality implementation

 Facilitate evidence driven operational efficiency and accelerate introduction and/or implementation of prioritized innovative approaches for sustainability and transition.

offres.description:
Manager, Pre-Financing Facility, NGFP, Finance & Administration - GL E - Defined Duration until December 2028 
The Manager, Pre-Financing Facility (PFF) is responsible for the strategic leadership, financial stewardship, and risk-adjusted performance of the Pre-Financing Facility (PFF), a financing portfolio established to support eligible transactions under the Non-Global Fund Financed Procurement (NGFP) framework.
The role has a matric reporting structure, operating under the technical and administrative oversight of the Head, Financial Accounting and Treasury Operations (FATO) and with strategic accountability to the Chief Financial Officer (CFO). This dual alignment reflects the position’s critical function in the stewardship, sustainability, and oversight of the PFF.
As the Facility's principal portfolio manager and financing authority, the incumbent is accountable for safeguarding the Facility's resources, preserving its sustainability, and ensuring that financing decisions deliver intended operational impact while remaining within approved risk, liquidity, and governance parameters.
The Manager, PFF is accountable for the development and operationalization of appropriate risk rating methodologies and the overall performance, sustainability, and risk management of the Pre-Financing Facility portfolio. The role acts as the Facility's designated portfolio owner, with responsibility for protecting resources, optimizing risk-adjusted portfolio performance, ensuring liquidity sufficiency, and maintaining compliance with approved governance and guarantee frameworks.
The incumbent leads the evaluation, structuring, approval, and ongoing management of financing transactions while maintaining a portfolio-wide view of asset quality, concentration risks, repayment trends, expected financing shortfalls, and emerging exposures. Beyond individual transactions, the Manager is responsible for ensuring that the Facility operates as a financially sound and sustainable financing mechanism capable of supporting strategic organizational objectives.
The role provides thought leadership and expert advice to senior management on financial risk, portfolio strategy, financing capacity utilization, and operational performance, and is the primary point of accountability for portfolio outcomes, governance reporting, stakeholder engagement, and continuous improvement of the Facility's operating model. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 Under the technical and administrative oversight of Head, FATO and the strategic accountability of the CFO, the Manager, PFF is responsible for:
 1. Facility Leadership and Governance 
 i. Lead the overall management and financial stewardship of the PFF.
 ii. Establish and maintain financing policies, underwriting standards, controls, delegated authorities, and monitoring frameworks
 iii. Ensure compliance with approved governance arrangements, guarantee agreements, and risk management requirements.
 iv. Provide strategic advice and recommendations to senior management on portfolio performance, risks, liquidity, and operational effectiveness.
 2. Transaction Assessment and Financing Decisions 
 i. Lead financial, fiduciary, and credit risk assessments for financing requests.
 ii. Assess borrower creditworthiness, repayment capacity, transaction structures, country risks, and other counterparty risks.
 iii. Approve, reject, or recommend financing transactions within delegated authority.
 iv. Ensure financing decisions are supported by robust analysis and transparent documentation.
 v. Escalate transactions requiring higher-level review or governance approval.
 3. Portfolio Risk Management 
 i. Manage the Facility as a portfolio of financing exposures.
 ii. Monitor portfolio quality, repayment performance, concentration risks, financing capacity utilization, liquidity sufficiency and expected financing shortfalls.
 iii. Oversee risk rating methodologies, watchlists, and early warning indicators.
 iv. Recommend risk mitigation actions and portfolio management measures as required.
 v. Ensure risks are identified, assessed, monitored, and reported appropriately.
 4. Recovery and Default Management 
 i. Lead monitoring, oversight and enforcement of decisions relating to overdue exposures, restructurings, recovery strategies, and default management.
 ii. Recommend provisions, impairments, guarantee claims, or write-offs as appropriate.
 iii. Coordinate with Grants Management Country Teams, Legal, Finance, Risk, and other stakeholders on recovery actions.
 5. Stakeholder Engagement and Reporting 
 i. Serve as the primary point of contact with guarantors, financing partners, auditors, and governance bodies.
 ii. Present portfolio performance, risk exposure, and financing activities to senior stakeholders.
 iii. Ensure timely, accurate, and transparent reporting.
 6. Team Leadership and Continuous Improvement 
 i. Lead, coach, and develop the PFF Specialist and any future team members.
 ii. Drive process optimization, automation, and operational excellence initiatives.
 iii. Foster a culture of accountability, collaboration, continuous learning, and risk awareness.
 Subject to change: These responsibilities may be refined as the NGFP Policy, financial framework, operational procedures, systems configuration and governance reporting arrangements are further operationalized. They are also subject to change by the Executive Director at any time at their sole discretion.

 Essential 
 Master's degree in finance, Accounting, Economics, Business Administration, Banking, Risk Management, or a related discipline. In lieu of a Master’s degree, a Bachelor’s degree in a relevant discipline may be considered where complemented by substantial professional experience directly relevant to the management of prefinancing facilities or comparable credit and financing activities.
 Professional certification such as CFA or equivalent.
 Desirable 
 Advanced training in sovereign-risk analysis, structured finance, project finance, treasury, asset-liability management, financial-institution risk management, credit risk analysis, credit underwriting, credit portfolio monitoring or related fields.
 Other relevant professional certifications such as CPA, CA, ACCA, FRM or equivalent.

 Demonstrated experience assessing and managing credit, financial, country, sovereign, and counterparty risks.
 Experience making or recommending lending, financing, investment, or credit decisions within a formal governance framework.
 Proven experience managing portfolios, liquidity risks, financial exposures, and performance monitoring.
 Experience engaging with senior executives, governance committees, auditors, financial institutions, donors, or development finance partners.

offres.description:
Specialist, Risk Management – NGFP Pre-Financing and Fiduciary Risk, Ethics & Risk Department - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2028 
The Specialist, Risk Management – NGFP Pre-Financing and Fiduciary Risk provides independent second-line assessment, challenge and oversight of financial and fiduciary risks arising from the Non-Global Fund-Financed Procurement Mechanism (NGFPM), with primary responsibility for independently reviewing pre-financing proposals submitted by the business for non-Global Fund-financed procurement, issuing documented risk opinions and, where expressly delegated, providing risk no-objection or clearance; and monitoring the risk profile of the Pre-Financing Facility (PFF).
Drawing on first-line due diligence and additional independent analysis as warranted, the incumbent independently assesses buyer and transaction risk, challenges underwriting assumptions and proposed financing terms, and provides documented second-line risk opinions on creditworthiness, repayment capacity, country and counterparty risk, exposure limits, concentration, guarantees, liquidity implications and other risk mitigants. The Specialist does not originate proposals, own or approve first-line financing decisions, execute transactions, maintain accounting records or recoveries, but evaluates whether these activities operate within approved policy, risk appetite, delegated authorities and control requirements.
The role maintains a portfolio-wide second-line view of exposures, risk ratings, concentrations, repayment performance, arrears, early-warning indicators, guarantee coverage and residual risk. It independently reviews actual outcomes against original assumptions, identifies emerging risks and control weaknesses, and recommends escalation, additional conditions, restrictions or corrective action where warranted.
The incumbent also supports the broader Finance, Fiduciary and Operations Risk portfolio through financial and fiduciary risk assessments, control and assurance reviews, incident and exception analysis, risk reporting and monitoring of remediation actions across corporate and grant-facing activities. 
Working closely with Finance, Treasury, Supply Operations, Grant Management, Legal, Ethics and assurance providers, the Specialist provides technically sound, concise and decision-useful advice to the Manager, Risk Management – Finance, Fiduciary and Operations. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 1. Provide independent second-line risk assessment of pre-financing proposals 
 (i) Review first-line assessments and independently assess buyer, payer and transaction-level credit, counterparty, sovereign, country and fiduciary risks, including financial capacity, fiscal and budget execution, public financial management constraints, political and macro-financial conditions, foreign-exchange exposure, transaction structure and proposed tenor.
 (ii) Challenge the completeness, quality and reasonableness of first-line due diligence, financial analysis, cash flow and repayment assumptions, risk ratings, exposure requests and proposed mitigants.
 (iii) Prepare clear, evidence-based second-line risk opinions and recommendations, including proposed conditions, limits, safeguards and escalation requirements, for consideration by the applicable decision authority.
 2. Provide independent oversight and challenge of underwriting standards and risk assessment methodologies 
 (i) Review and challenge risk assessment methodologies, underwriting criteria, scorecards, due-diligence standards, exposure limits, concentration thresholds, repayment structures and early-warning triggers to support consistent and risk-sensitive decisions.
 (ii) Independently assess the adequacy of proposed risk mitigations, including guarantees, funded or unfunded risk-sharing arrangements, first-loss structures and other credit enhancements, considering their effectiveness, enforceability and monitoring arrangements.
 (iii) Use portfolio outcomes, stress scenarios, incidents and assurance findings to recommend improvements to risk methodologies, thresholds and control requirements as the Facility matures and evolves.
 3. Monitor portfolio risk, repayment performance and emerging deterioration 
 (i)     Maintain an independent second-line portfolio-wide view of approved and utilized exposures, risk ratings, buyer and country concentrations, maturities, repayment performance, arrears, guarantee capacity, exceptions and residual risk.
 (ii)   Define and monitor key risk indicators, watchlists and early-warning information before and after payment due dates, and recommend timely escalation, additional conditions, restrictions, suspension of new pre-financing or other corrective measures where risk increases.
 (iii) Perform periodic and event-driven reassessments and compare actual portfolio performance with original underwriting assumptions to identify rating migration, emerging vulnerabilities and lessons for future decisions.
 4. Oversee NGFPM fiduciary risks and the control environment 
 (i) Independently review and assess the design and through targeted testing or assurance evidence, the operating effectiveness of key controls covering financial onboarding, funding-source verification, fund segregation and ring-fencing, delegated authorities, transaction approval, exposure-cap utilization, documentation, repayment monitoring, reconciliations, default escalation, recoveries, exception management and risk reporting.
 (ii) Review material policies, procedures, systems and process changes and provide constructive second-line challenge on control ownership, segregation of duties, evidence requirements, data integrity, escalation pathways and consistency across NGFP documentation.
 (iii) Undertake targeted second-line reviews and thematic assessments, support assurance planning, and monitor remediation of significant control weaknesses, incidents, exceptions and audit findings.
 5. Deliver risk analytics, reporting and governance support 
 (i) Produce accurate and decision-oriented risk analysis on portfolio quality, concentrations, repayment trends, arrears, expected loss drivers, guarantee coverage, control performance and emerging risks.
 (ii) Provide risk inputs for management and governance reporting and communicate complex underwriting, sovereign and fiduciary-risk matters clearly to technical and senior stakeholders.
 (iii) Maintain complete and auditable records of second-line assessments, challenge, opinions, risk clearances where delegated, recommendations, decisions, exceptions and follow-up actions.
 6. Support broader financial and fiduciary risk management 
 (i) Contribute to financial and fiduciary risk assessments, control reviews and assurance activities across corporate and grant-facing operations, including liquidity, foreign exchange, fraud, financial controls, public financial management and fiduciary arrangements.
 (ii) Analyze risk events, incidents and exceptions; track mitigation and remediation actions; and support timely escalation and reporting of material risks.
 (iii) Develop practical tools, guidance and knowledge products, and build constructive relationships with first-line and assurance functions while preserving second-line independence and accountability.

Specialist, In-Country Supply Chain – Design and Delivery Models, Supply Operations - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029 
The Global Fund aims to accelerate the end of AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria as epidemics, while increasing access to quality-assured health products and services at affordable and sustainable prices. Within the Secretariat, Supply Operations plays a central role in sourcing, procurement, quality assurance and supply chain matters, including strategy formulation and implementation, policy development, innovation, sustainability, new product introduction and country capacity building. The In-Country Supply Chain (ICSC) team leads the Global Fund's work to strengthen national health supply chains, particularly in countries with under-developed supply chain infrastructure and management systems, so that health products procured through Global Fund grants reach people reliably, efficiently and sustainably.
The Specialist, In-Country Supply Chain – Design and Delivery Models leads the ICSC team's work on private sector engagement in national health supply chains. Under the supervision of the Manager, In-Country Supply Chain Strategy, Policy and Initiatives, the Specialist drives the design and adoption of efficient, sustainable delivery models, covering third- and fourth-party logistics (3PL/4PL) outsourcing, alternate delivery channels through private pharmacies and drug shops, market intelligence across the total (public and private) market, and whole-market introduction of new health products.
Public delivery channels alone will not achieve the coverage, efficiency and resilience that national supply chains require. The Specialist helps countries harness private sector capacity, from professionalized logistics providers to retail pharmacy networks, to extend access to quality-assured health products, reduce costs and accelerate the introduction of new products such as long-acting HIV prevention, near-point-of-care TB diagnostics, novel antimalarials and more. The role contributes to the delivery of related Catalytic Investments.
The position requires strong expertise in logistics outsourcing and contracting, private sector delivery channels, market analytics and new product introduction, combined with the ability to work credibly with both governments and commercial actors. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 The main responsibilities of the Specialist, In-Country Supply Chain – Design and Delivery Models include:
 1. Lead logistics outsourcing and 3PL/4PL market development 
 Support countries to professionalize downstream logistics through the private sector, by:
 Advising governments and Country Teams on outsourcing strategy, including make-or-buy analysis, network segmentation and phasing of outsourced warehousing and distribution.
 Supporting the design and execution of competitive 3PL/4PL tenders, including specifications, service level agreements, pricing structures and evaluation approaches.
 Strengthening contract and performance management of logistics providers, including KPI frameworks, performance-based payment mechanisms and dispute resolution.
 Shaping downstream logistics provider markets, including actions to broaden supplier participation, reduce costs and improve service quality over successive contracting rounds.
 2. Develop alternate delivery channels through the private sector 
 Extend access to health products beyond traditional public service delivery points, by:
 Designing and supporting implementation of delivery models that leverage private pharmacies, drug shops and comparable retail outlets for the distribution of quality-assured HTM and related health products.
 Overseeing country pilots and scale-up of private channel models, including in priority geographies, with attention to quality assurance, pricing, reporting and equity of access.
 Addressing the enabling environment for private channel participation, including accreditation, regulation, data reporting and links to national insurance and reimbursement mechanisms, in coordination with the ICSC financing workstream.
 Documenting evidence on channel performance, cost and access outcomes to inform Global Fund policy and country investment decisions.
 3. Build market intelligence across the total market 
 Ensure decisions are informed by robust intelligence on both public and private channels, by:
 Developing and maintaining market intelligence on private sector distribution landscapes, logistics provider markets, channel volumes, pricing and service coverage in priority countries.
 Analyzing total market dynamics for key product categories to identify access gaps, market failure risks and opportunities for market shaping actions, in coordination with the Supply Operations NextGen Market Shaping strategy.
 Translating market intelligence into actionable briefs for Country Teams, Secretariat leadership and partners.
 4. Drive whole-market new product introduction 
 Accelerate equitable introduction of new health products across all channels, by:
 Developing channel strategies for new product introduction that span public and private delivery, including for long-acting HIV prevention products, new TB diagnostics and treatments, and next-generation malaria tools.
 Advising countries on the supply chain and distribution readiness required for introduction and scale-up, including demand planning, channel selection and last-mile delivery arrangements.
 Coordinating with sourcing, market shaping, Technical Advice and Partnerships, Grant Management Division, and technical partners to align introduction plans across the market.
 5. Deliver Catalytic Investments and coordinate with stakeholders 
 Ensure effective delivery of catalytic funding and coherent stakeholder engagement, by:
 Managing assigned workplans and deliverables under Catalytic Investments, including technical partner oversight, monitoring of progress and synthesis of results.
 Providing structured guidance and analysis to Country Teams on private sector engagement questions arising in country dialogue, funding requests, grant making and implementation.
 Serving as an effective interface with other Supply Operations teams, the Grant Management Division, Technical Advice and Partnerships, Risk and other relevant functions.
 Engaging with external partners, including donors, technical assistance providers, logistics industry actors and private sector associations, and contributing to internal and external training and guidance.
 Subject to change by the Executive Director at any time at their sole discretion. 
 Qualifications 
 Essential: 
 Advanced university degree in supply chain management, logistics, business administration, engineering, public health or another relevant field.
 Desirable: 
 Qualification in business, engineering and/or supply chain.
 Experience 
 Essential: 
 Substantial relevant professional experience (typically eight to ten years) in supply chain and logistics at international level, including significant private sector or private-sector-facing experience.
 Demonstrated experience in logistics outsourcing, including tender design, contracting, service level agreements and performance management of 3PL/4PL providers.
 Experience designing or implementing delivery models involving private channels such as pharmacies, drug shops or retail networks, ideally for health products.
 Experience in market analysis or market intelligence, and in translating analysis into strategy and investment decisions.
 Proven experience operating in complex organizational environments and working across public and private stakeholders.
 Desirable: 
 Experience in both public and private sector supply chain environments, especially in pharma, retail, warehousing and distribution, and/or fast-moving consumer goods.
 Experience with new product introduction and launch across multiple channels.
 Experience working on the African continent.
 Competencies

Within the Secretariat, Supply Operations plays a central role in sourcing, procurement, quality assurance and supply chain matters, including strategy formulation and implementation, policy development, innovation, sustainability, new product introduction and country capacity building. The In-Country Supply Chain (ICSC) team leads the Global Fund's work to strengthen national health supply chains, particularly in countries with under-developed supply chain infrastructure and management systems, so that health products procured through Global Fund grants reach people reliably, efficiently and sustainably.
The Specialist, Sustainable ICSC Financing strengthens the links between supply chain and health financing. Under the supervision of the Manager, In-Country Supply Chain Strategy & Policy, the Specialist leads the ICSC team's work on Public Financial Management (PFM) use cases for supply chains (budget design, execution and expenditure tracking), the integration of HIV, TB and malaria (HTM) products and services into national health insurance schemes, and supply chain costing and cost optimization.
As Global Fund grant financing evolves and countries assume greater responsibility for financing their supply chains, the Specialist generates the cost transparency, financing analysis and PFM linkages that countries need to make credible domestic financing cases, budget realistically for procurement and supply management functions, and progressively embed health products into sustainable domestic financing pathways. The role works closely with the Public Financial Management and Health Finance teams within the Finance department, the Grant Management Division and external partners, and contributes to the delivery of related Catalytic Investments.
The position requires strong expertise at the intersection of supply chain management and health financing, including costing, budgeting, public financial management, health insurance and value-for-money analysis. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 The main responsibilities of the Specialist, Sustainable ICSC Financing include:
 1. Lead the supply chain and health financing agenda 
 Serve as the ICSC team's technical lead on the links between supply chain and health financing, by:
 •         Developing and championing PFM use cases for supply chains, including budget structures that adequately reflect supply chain functions (storage, distribution, human resources, systems), budget execution and expenditure tracking for supply chain operations, and fiscal transparency in health product financing.
 •         Supporting countries and Country Teams to identify and close supply chain financing gaps, including through financing gap analyses that map full supply chain operating costs against financing sources (Global Fund grants, domestic budgets, other donors, in-country revenues generated from business models).
 •         Ensuring supply chain priorities are reflected in funding design, co-financing commitments, value-for-money considerations, sustainability and transition planning, and broader health systems financing dialogue.
 •         Coordinating closely with the Public Financial Management (PFM) and Health Finance teams within Finance, including on the interface with the PFM Catalytic Investment, to ensure coherent, complementary support to countries.
 2. Drive supply chain costing, cost benchmarking and optimization 
 Build the cost evidence base for efficient, sustainably financed supply chains, by:
 •         Leading supply chain cost benchmarking work across the portfolio, including methodology, data collection, analysis and cross-country comparison of storage, distribution and overhead costs.
 •         Supporting deployment and further development of supply chain costing tools and models, and their use by countries, Country Teams and partners to inform budgeting, outsourcing decisions and network optimization.
 •         Identifying and quantifying optimization opportunities (network design, delivery frequency, channel choices, integration of vertical supply chains) and translating them into actionable recommendations and investment cases.
 •         Contributing costing and efficiency analysis to grant design, funding request review and reprogramming decisions.
 3. Support integration of HTM products into national health insurance schemes 
 Advance sustainable domestic financing pathways for health products, by:
 •         Supporting selected countries in designing or expanding health insurance benefits packages to include HTM products and related services, including analysis of budget impact, provider payment mechanisms and implications for product flows, claims and reimbursement.
 •         Analyzing the supply chain implications of insurance-based financing (accreditation of dispensing points, private channel participation, data and traceability requirements) and advising countries and Country Teams accordingly.
 •         Documenting and disseminating learning across the portfolio, in coordination with the Health Finance team and technical partners.
 4. Deliver and manage related Catalytic Investments 
 Contribute to the effective design, delivery and measurement of catalytic funding, by:
 •         Managing assigned workplans and deliverables under Catalytic Investments, including technical partner selection, contracting inputs, oversight of deliverables, and monitoring of progress and results.
 •         Preparing briefing materials, syntheses and internal recommendations for Secretariat leadership, governance bodies and donors.
 •         Enabling cross-portfolio learning, identifying best practices and supporting their scale-up across countries.
 5. Provide advisory support and coordinate with stakeholders 
 Act as a recognized source of expertise within and beyond the Secretariat, by:
 •         Providing structured guidance and analysis to Country Teams on supply chain financing, costing and optimization questions arising in country dialogue, funding requests, grant making and implementation.
 •         Serving as an effective interface with other Supply Operations teams, the Grant Management Division, Health Finance, Technical Advice and Partnerships, Risk and other relevant functions.
 •         Engaging with external partners, including the Gates Foundation, the World Bank (including Global Financing Facility), WHO, bilateral partners and technical assistance providers, on supply chain financing and costing matters.
 •         Contributing to internal and external training and guidance on Global Fund in-country supply chain policies, tools and approaches.
 Subject to change by the Executive Director at any time at their sole discretion. 
 Qualifications 
 Essential: 
 Advanced university degree in economics, health economics, finance, business administration, public health, supply chain management or another relevant field.
 Desirable: 
 Additional qualification in health financing, public financial management or supply chain management.
 Experience 
 Essential: 
 Substantial relevant professional experience (typically eight to ten years) in health financing, health economics and/or supply chain management at international level, especially in low- and middle-income countries.
 Demonstrated experience working at the intersection of operational systems and financing decisions, such as supply chain costing, cost-benchmarking, budget and expenditure analysis, investment design or value-for-money analysis.
 Experience with public financial management processes in the health sector, including budget formulation, execution and expenditure tracking.

Implementation Specialist, Integration & Quality of Services - GL D - Defined Duration until December 2029 (French Speaking) 
The Global Fund aims to accelerate the end of AIDS, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria as epidemics. The organization invests more than US$4 billion per year to support programs run by local experts in countries and communities most in need. Since 2020, through the COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM), additional funding has been made available to support countries to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 and build resilient community and public health systems. 
The Global Fund’s Grant Management Division (GMD), in collaboration with teams across the Global Fund Secretariat, is responsible for the overall management of the Global Fund’s grant investments at country and regional level, driving impact in implementing countries. It provides leadership and strategic direction to the Global Fund’s country operations and drives the translation of the GF strategy into operational milestones at global, regional, and country portfolio level, including signing grants, making disbursements, regular portfolio monitoring and oversight. It works in a complex and rapidly evolving environment with implementing partners, including Principal Recipients (PRs), sub-recipients (SRs), Country Coordinating Mechanisms (CCM), in-country health sector and humanitarian clusters, multiple stakeholders from public, private sectors and communities to drive success on the ground and manage the growth in portfolio investments value, expanding breadth and depth of program and systems strengthening interventions, sophistication of program design, data driven decision making, differentiated approaches, intensified program quality focus, introduction of new health products, services and interventions.
The Global Fund’s approach to ending HIV, TB and Malaria (HTM) is underpinned by investments in building resilient and sustainable systems for health (RSSH). As part of a transition to more integrated, people-centered quality services, the Global Fund aims to integrate HTM service provision and other relevant services into primary health care (PHC) by strengthening community and primary health care platforms. This includes emphasizing the role of community health workers, promoting better integration of service delivery, including of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services at all levels, and digital health.
Various countries have planned for the introduction and/or scale-up of such approaches through prioritized portfolio investments, including in challenging operating environments where barriers to services are often intensified.
The Implementation Specialist, Integration & Quality of Services will play a crucial role in incentivizing and facilitating this country-level work and will collaborate at country and regional level with a multitude of technical and development partners, national technical leads, decision makers, community actors and other key stakeholders who support the vision of integrated, people-centered quality services. 
The Implementation Specialist, Integration & Quality of Services will be based in a regional team in the Grant Management Division (GMD) and will collaborate with Public Health Monitoring & Evaluation Specialists (PHME) and other members of Country Teams, other Implementation Specialists in the region, and relevant functional Specialists within the Technical Advice and Partnerships Department (TAP) and Community Rights and Gender Department (CRG) to advance grant implementation and achievement of results for the assigned country portfolios. The Implementation Specialist will also liaise with the Private Sector Engagement Department (PSED) on donor communication, reporting, and other engagement as relevant.
The Implementation Specialist, Integration & Quality will contribute to the design and implementation of proactive operational planning for investments in high-quality, integrated health services, including for SRH, under Global Fund grants, regular monitoring and assessments of performance against set milestones and targets, ongoing problem solving, iterative lessons learned and integration in adaptive improvement and acceleration plans. The Implementation Specialist will drive the continued collaboration, joint investment opportunities and alignment with other donors. S/he will provide guidance on resources, training and coordination of relevant technical assistance (TA) to improve the plans for effective and efficient implementation of community health worker, SRH, and related digital health interventions. The Implementation Specialist will also lead the development and socialization of a learning agenda for implementation of integrated service delivery. 
 Key Responsibilities 
 The main responsibilities of the Implementation Specialist, Integration & Quality of Services include:
 1. Investments guidance, planning and engagement 
 Provide guidance, in close collaboration with relevant technical teams, on the design and ongoing adaptation of grant investments and strategies to advance the uptake, roll-out and/or scale-up of integrated approaches and platforms, innovative tools including but not limited to digital health, and best practices to improve access to and delivery of high-quality, integrated health services.
 Lead engagement with principal recipients (PRs) and other key actors in the in-country implementation ecosystem, including technical agency leads, community actors, key decision makers, and country level technical and financing partners to elaborate vision of success and implementation roadmaps, including key milestones and metrics for monitoring progress and results achievements in prioritized investment areas (e.g primary healthcare integration, SRH, digital health).
 Oversee operational assessments in response to country-specific needs, to enable accelerated operationalization, execution and/or scale up of interventions in prioritized investment areas.
 Identify key stakeholders and facilitate partnership engagement to advance integration and quality of services at country level, including the establishment of new or expanded relationships with wider group of national stakeholders working to strengthen primary and community health platforms.
 Facilitate dialogues to align priorities, integrate innovations (e.g. integrated service packages, digital health), link with broader health reforms (e.g. universal health coverage, social protection) and enhance in-country mechanisms for governance, monitoring, execution and technical support for related investments.
 2. Facilitate and mobilize support for high quality implementation 
 Oversee execution of in-country implementation roadmaps, including regular tracking and reporting on progress, timely escalation, trouble shooting, and problem-solving.
 Lead implementation gaps analysis, identification of critical bottlenecks in implementation of prioritized investments, and facilitate the development of adaptive action plans for accelerated implementation.
 Map, mobilize and coordinate TA needs and opportunities as relevant to address implementation bottlenecks and accelerate integrated, high quality service delivery in prioritized investment areas, leveraging institutional and in-country resources, including those provided through Strategic Initiatives (SI) and Centrally Managed Limited Investments (CMLI).
 In coordination with relevant functional Specialists in TAP, oversee development of integrated TA plans, act as a focal point for ensuring TA offer meets country demand and key portfolio priorities, monitor execution of TA, and contribute to quality assurance of TA products.
 Represent GMD in cross-departmental program implementation team to ensure alignment on critical delivery and reporting milestones, regular follow up, and coordination across teams working to operationalize donor partnerships, as relevant.

 The IRC has been operating in South Sudan since 1989 and is registered as an international NGO. IRC currently delivers multi sectoral programming directly and through partners across seven states and two administrative areas. These include Northern Bahr el Ghazal, covering Aweil East, Aweil West, and Aweil South counties, Unity State, covering Rubkona, Koch, and Panyijiar counties, Upper Nile State, covering Maban, Renk, Panyikang, Nasir, Ulang, and Panylgang counties, Lakes State, covering Rumbek Centre, Rumbek East, and Yirol West counties, Central Equatoria, covering Juba, Yei, and Kajokeji counties, Eastern Equatoria, covering Kapoeta East, Jonglei, covering Ayod, Twic East, Uror, Akobo counties, as well as Abyei Administrative Area and Ruweng Administrative Area, including Pariang County and Ajoung Thok and Pamir refugee camps.
 Background and objectives of Education for all South Sudan(EFASS) 
South Sudan has one of the world's most fragile education systems, with approximately 2.8 to 3 million children, representing around 60 to 70 percent of the school-age population, out of school. Foundational literacy and numeracy outcomes remain critically low, with less than 10 percent of children achieving minimum reading competency. Years of conflict, accelerating climate shocks, and government education expenditure under 3 percent of the national budget have created an entrenched crisis. Girls and children with disabilities are disproportionately affected by these barriers, with harmful gender norms and stigma further limiting their access to education. 
 EFASS is a £27 million, four-year programme (April 2026 to March 2030), designed to deliver five interlinked outcomes. These include improving access, retention, and progression for the most marginalised out-of-school children, particularly girls and children with disabilities in conflict and climate-affected areas. The programme also targets improved foundational learning outcomes in literacy and numeracy, strengthened delivery of inclusive and climate-adaptive education approaches by teachers and facilitators, improved education data and evidence for decision-making through a national Learning Outcomes and Quality Assessment, as well as strengthened pathways for system uptake and sustainability beyond EFASS.
 Scope of Work 
The Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEAL) Lead serves as a member of the Programme's Senior Management Team and is responsible for developing and implementing the programme's MEAL strategy in accordance with organisational, FCDO, and international best-practice requirements. Working closely with the Team Leader, Deputy Team Leader, and technical staff, the MEAL Lead ensures that relevant data is collected, analysed, and used to inform management and design decisions.
 The MEAL Lead develops and manages a monitoring and evaluation system across all programme components that leverages qualitative and quantitative methods to measure progress and evaluate impact against the programme's five interlinked outcomes. The postholder ensures that results from monitoring, the Learning Outcomes and Quality Assessment, and lesson learning systematically feed into programme implementation through adaptive management principles. This includes overseeing quarterly reviews to assess cost-effectiveness and learning outcomes, with underperforming models redesigned or discontinued through a fail-fast approach. The MEAL Lead ensures rigorous documentation of evidence on effective models for fragile and conflict-affected contexts to inform future pooled donor investments and national education recovery planning.
 The MEAL Lead communicates information obtained through monitoring and evaluation activities to programme staff and external stakeholders, including FCDO, the Ministry of General Education and Instruction, and sector coordination bodies, to enable informed decision-making. The postholder ensures data collection processes function across all activity locations to provide quality, timely data, regularly performs data quality assessments, spearheading analysis of all datasets for effective tracking of planned activities by EFASS and conducts site visits to provide technical assistance to the downstream partners.
 The MEAL Lead produces monthly, quarterly, semi-annual, and annual reports as required and ensures all data is disaggregated by gender and disability status using the Washington Group set of questions in line with global best practice.
The MEAL Lead will provide strategic and technical leadership for Outcome 4, guiding the programme’s evidence agenda and ensuring the Research and MIS Data teams deliver high quality, decision ready outputs. The postholder will lead the design and delivery of the national LOQA and oversee the programme MIS and data governance, including partner data integration, validation, and development of practical dashboards and analysis products. The role will translate LOQA and pilot evidence into clear recommendations and learning products that shape implementation choices and system pathways, while strengthening evidence uptake with MoGEI and sector stakeholders, and ensuring alignment with wider sector priorities and financing initiatives such as GPE, ECW, and the World Bank.The MEAL Lead trains and supervises a team of MEAL staff to collect high-quality programme data and contributes to staff and partner capacity building on MEAL best practices. This is a senior position requiring outstanding leadership, strategic thinking, and organisational and team-building skills.

 1. About IRC 
 The International Rescue Committee (IRC) is an international non-governmental organization. IRC helps people whose lives and livelihoods are shattered by conflict and disaster to survive, recover, and gain control of their future. IRC has built expertise in supporting societies in their transition to sustainable development, with a focus on assisting subnational institutions to deliver basic social services. The IRC has an exceptional capacity to build the technical capacity of subnational institutions and deliver quality services in sectors including health care, violence prevention and response (protection, including child protection and women’s protection and empowerment (WPE/GBV)), education, economic recovery and development, governance, and research and learning. As a recognized global leader in protection programming, IRC is committed to addressing the world’s humanitarian crises and development challenges through context appropriate, gender transformative, evidence-based, outcome-driven interventions that bring real change to the lives of our clients.
  2. Context 
 The humanitarian crises in Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen remain among the most complex globally, characterized by protracted conflict, economic collapse, and weakened health and protection systems. Women, children (boys and particularly girls), and marginalized groups face heightened risks of gender-based violence (GBV), limited access to basic sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR), and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). The IRC has been implementing integrated protection and health interventions to address these needs, guided by feminist principles and localization strategies.
 Syria (SY):  considered one of the largest and most complex displacement crises in the world. More than ten million Syrians remain forcibly displaced, including more than 3.5 million refugees hosted in Lebanon, Jordan, and other neighboring countries. Since the fall of the Assad-led government in December 2024, more than 1.1 million refugees and 1.9 million internally displaced persons have reportedly returned to their areas of origin. Yet despite this increase in the return movements, most displaced Syrians are unlikely to return in the near term, with many citing ongoing concerns over safety, access to services, durable solutions, limited civil documentation, and scarce economic opportunities. Lebanon (LB): Five years of economic crisis have left LB with 3.9M people requiring humanitarian aid. Needs are particularly severe in North and Akkar, remote, underserved, and hosting more than 357,000 Syrian refugees.  IRC/partner, GBV Working Group, and Child Protection AoR data/findings show declining access to essential services and decreasing protections, particularly for women & children (girls and boys).  IRC studies also find that lack of documentation for those who are discriminated against, or cannot afford or properly follow legal processes, profoundly affects women, limiting movement for fear of interrogation or detention. Lebanon continues to face overlapping humanitarian pressures driven by ongoing insecurity, economic collapse, and large-scale displacement. Despite a November 2024 ceasefire, hostilities and violations persist, contributing to widespread destruction and leaving over 860,000 people internally displaced, with essential services severely disrupted across multiple regions. Akkar and North Lebanon—already among the country’s poorest areas—have absorbed substantial new arrivals from Syria, hosting over 17,000 newly displaced individuals in Akkar alone, many living in overcrowded shelters or with host families amid significant gaps in WASH, shelter, and protection services. Simultaneously, return movements to Syria have increased following political shifts there, with more than 146,000 Syrians returning from Lebanon since December 2024; however, conditions in Syria remain unstable, and many returnees face obstacles related to documentation, housing, and livelihoods, raising concerns about the sustainability and voluntariness of returns.
 Yemen (YM): W&Gs in YM face acute humanitarian and protection needs, resulting from ten years of conflict. An estimated 21.6M people need humanitarian and protection aid, with 6.1M having catastrophic need, and 4.5M internally displaced (77% women and children)
 3. Project Background 
 The IRC’s Regional Integrated Protection and Health Response project (2024–2026) aims to improve safety, health, and well-being for women, children (girls and boys), and vulnerable populations in Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen. The project integrates GBV prevention and response, SRHR services, MHPSS, and child protection (CP) interventions, alongside capacity strengthening of local actors. The CAD 8 million initiative targets over 127,000 beneficiaries and emphasizes gender equality, GEDI, accountability, and conflict sensitivity.
 IRC and partners propose a critical two-year humanitarian intervention in the heavily crisis-impacted regions of northeast Syria, northern Lebanon and Lahj, Yemen, based on the following Theory of Change: IF women and children are able to access quality, lifesaving integrated  GBV, SRH, MHPSS and CP services, AND IF social norms support women and girls’ rights and promote women and girls’ SRHR and condemn GBV, AND IF women-led organizations (WLOs), CBOs, and health systems are strengthened to support SRH rights and leadership to respond to and prevent GBV, THEN women and children will be empowered and safe from GBV, and can achieve their SRH and protection rights ( See annex 1 for full Logical Model ).
